meta: Thinking of installing a gas water heater yourself? We explain the gas, vent and strapping steps and when to hire a plumber in Oakley, CA. Call (888) 910-8644.
lead: Installing a gas water heater in Oakley, CA joins gas, venting, water and earthquake bracing in one closet. For most homeowners the answer is to hire a licensed plumber and keep the gas side out of your own hands.
intro: A gas water heater installation is the job of removing the old tank, setting a new one, and connecting its gas line, flue, cold and hot water lines, temperature and pressure relief valve and seismic straps. In Oakley, CA that work happens in a home served by Diablo Water District for water and PG&E for gas, in Contra Costa County.

Some steps are within reach of a handy owner, but a mistake on the gas or vent side can put carbon monoxide or a gas leak inside the house. This guide walks through each connection, where homeowners get into trouble, and how to decide who should do the work.

sections.h2: Should a homeowner install a gas water heater at all?
paras: Most people can lift the old tank out with a helper, and many can fit a new one into the same spot. The trouble is that a gas water heater is not an ordinary fixture. It burns fuel, sends exhaust up a flue, and holds dozens of gallons of hot water under pressure, so every connection has to be right before the first firing.

A swap that looks simple can hide a corroded gas shutoff, a flue pipe that no longer rises steadily, or a relief valve that dumps hot water onto the floor. A licensed plumber checks these as routine. Our [[water-heater-installation|water heater installation]] page explains how a new unit is sited, vented and connected if you want to see the full scope.

sections.h2: Six connections that decide whether the install is safe
paras: Each item below is a place where a rushed or untested job causes trouble later.

items.d: A fresh connector or rigid pipe, a shutoff valve you can reach, and a sediment trap where the setup calls for one. Every joint is tested for leaks before the burner is lit, never judged by smell alone.
The vent pipe has to rise steadily to the outdoors, with tight joints and the clearances printed in the manufacturer's manual. Poor draft pulls exhaust back into the room.
A gas burner needs fresh air to burn cleanly. A sealed closet or garage corner without enough openings can starve the flame and produce carbon monoxide.
The temperature and pressure relief valve is the last safety device if the thermostat fails. Its discharge pipe should run downward to a safe spot, with no cap, plug or upward bend.
On a closed water system, heated water has nowhere to expand and pressure climbs. A small expansion tank absorbs the swing and protects the tank, fixtures and supply lines.
California expects water heaters to be braced against earthquake movement. The local note below gives the law that applies.

sections.h2: If you smell gas, stop and leave first
paras: Gas safety comes before any plumbing question. Gas odor near the heater means you walk out first, dial 911 from the yard or street, and then ring PG&E at 1-800-743-5000. Do not flip switches, light anything or hunt for the leak yourself. Call a plumber only after emergency crews say the house is safe.

If you close the gas valve yourself, only PG&E can restore service, so a shutoff is a pause and not a repair. A pilot that keeps going out, a lazy yellow flame, or soot around the draft hood are also reasons to stop and have the unit inspected, even with no odor.

sections.h2: What a proper swap looks like, start to finish
paras: The order below is the general sequence. Your unit's manual controls the details, and any step that surprises you is a reason to pause.
bullets: Shut off the gas and the cold supply, then drain the old tank
Disconnect the old unit and note how the vent and gas were routed
Set the new tank level on a stable base and fit the strapping
Connect water lines, expansion tank and the relief valve discharge
Reconnect gas, leak test every joint, then light the burner by the manual
Check draft at the flue and confirm hot water at a faucet

localnote.source_type: Bay Area Air Quality Management District, California Health and Safety Code, City of Oakley, PG&E
paras: Our county is inside the Bay Area Air Quality Management District, which regulates the emissions of replacement gas tanks. Rule 9-6 has limited nitrogen oxide from gas water heaters for decades, and the zero-NOx standard for new residential gas units, once set for January 1, 2027, was delayed to January 2028 by amendments the Board adopted on November 4, 2026.

A Board vote on November 4, 2026 pushed that date back to January 2028 and added exemptions. Look up the date and any exemption that fits your home at baaqmd.gov before you commit to a gas model. The rule applies to new units at the time of replacement, not to the heater you already own.

State law covers strapping. Health and Safety Code 19211 says new and replacement water heaters, and existing residential ones, must be braced, anchored or strapped, and tanks of 120 gallons or less usually use a pre-engineered kit. We cannot promise either way whether a gas heater swap needs a City permit, so put that question to the Building Division staff by phone before the install date.

The permit counter is at 3231 Main Street, and either you or your contractor can apply. We cover Oakley and nearby towns, as the [[service-area|service area]] page shows. Neighbors in [[plumber-brentwood-ca|Brentwood]] live under the same Air District rules, though their permit questions go to the City of Brentwood Building Division.

faqs.q: Is it legal to install my own gas water heater in California?
a: The City of Oakley's website does not list water heater work specifically, and permit rules vary. Call the City permit staff before you start and write down what they tell you.
Whatever the answer on permits, the gas and vent connections are the riskiest parts for an amateur, and a leak test needs to pass before the burner runs.

faqs.q: What signs mean I should replace the tank instead of repairing it?
a: Water seeping from the tank body, rust at the base, rusty hot water and repeated repairs all point toward replacement. A leak through the steel shell cannot be patched.
A failed thermostat, igniter or gas control is a different story and often worth repairing, which is why a quick inspection comes first.

faqs.q: Do I need an expansion tank with a new gas water heater?
a: It depends on whether your home is a closed system, meaning something such as a check valve or pressure reducing valve keeps expanded water from flowing back to the street.
A plumber can test for this at the time of the install and size the tank to match your heater.

faqs.q: Can I switch from gas to electric or a heat pump during the swap?
a: Often yes. The deciding factors are electrical panel capacity, floor space, and how a condensate line would drain.
The Air District rules discussed above apply only to gas units, so a fuel change sidesteps them. A plumber can check your panel and closet before you order anything.

faqs.q: Will the Air District rule stop me from buying a gas water heater in Oakley?
a: The amended date came out of that November 2026 vote. January 1, 2027 was the earlier schedule, and the amendments move the start to January 2028 with some exemptions.
The district website carries the rule text as it now stands.
